title: The Plan Board
concept: After this one you can place a life story's Don'ts, Musts, how-tos and plan on the Plan Board, name the decision under them, and propose a new line that can be acted on this month.
bookIdea: A script matrix is a diagram of the messages each parent sends, the counterscript from the parent's Parent, the injunctions from the parent's Child and the program that shows how, plus the decision the child makes in answer.
bookSource: Scripts People Live, ch. 4, 6 and 21; TA Today, ch. 13

opener.setting: Sunday, 9:40am. The Corner Table, the back table. Nadia has printed Gran's life story on one long sheet, and the Plan Board beside it is still blank.

lines.text: “Gran's board first, then yours. Read her story for the Don'ts and the Musts, and don't rush the last few lines.”
lines.cue: sliding the printed sheet across the table

lines.text: “Sorry, sorry, I'm late. Is it the one with the grid? I hate the grid.”
lines.cue: dropping into a chair with a mug in each hand

opener.ask: Build Gran's Plan Board first, and find the decision she made as a girl. Then propose a new line she could act on, and build your own from your Plan Board.

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro:
Gran's life story, in her own words.
I was the middle one of four girls, in a town with one bus a day.
My mother ran the house like a clock. She never sat down while the rest of us ate.
When I said I wanted to finish school, she said, “Sit down. Your opinion isn't needed.”
My father was a quiet man. When we cried, he said, “Be strong. Let the neighbours see that we are fine.”
He also said, “You're still my little girl. Stay home where I can see you.”
My mother said, “Be the good one. Never cause trouble for the family.”
So I was the good one. I did what I was told, and I was never the loud one.
I married at nineteen. My husband was kind, and he was away for work half the year.
We had two children. I did their lunches and their homework.
My husband died when the youngest was eleven. I did the building society and the school fees.
People said, “Gran, you're so strong.” I was pleased, and also tired.
Every time I wanted something for myself, I put it on the list for later.
The sewing class, and the course in accounts. Later, I said. Later.
“I'll live properly once the children are settled,” I told myself, and I believed it.
The children grew up and did well. My son went to Canada for work and rings on Sundays, most weeks.
My daughter has a flat of her own and little time for her old mother.
I thought, once they are both settled, I'll go to the temple every morning and sit for an hour.
But there is always one more thing. The knees, and the letter from the building society.
Leo comes on Saturdays. I make his tea at four, sweet, the way he likes it.
Once he showed me a drawing with twelve wheels. I put it under the newspaper and said I'd look later.
He stopped bringing me drawings after that. It is my fault, and it is nobody's fault.
Now I wonder what I would have done with the years I put on the list.
I wonder if the children were ever the reason, or only the excuse.
I'm sixty-four. The knees are bad and the list is still long.
Nobody asked me what I wanted. I didn't ask either, because the answer came too late to be useful.

items.prompt: Gran's life story, line by line. Put each line on the Plan Board.

items.why: Her mother's message is that Gran doesn't count. It is a Don't: she is told not to be important, and she learns to take the chair at the edge.

items.text: “Be the good one. Never cause trouble for the family.”
items.why: This is a Must. It says 'be good' as a condition: keep the rule and you are safe. It comes in plain words, which Musts usually do, and it is a rule she has to keep.

items.text: “You're still my little girl. Stay home where I can see you.”
items.why: Her father's message keeps her small. It is a Don't: don't grow up, and don't go where he cannot see you.

items.text: “Be strong. Let the neighbours see that we are fine.”
items.why: Another Must, this time from her father. 'Be strong' is a rule with a condition in it: show the family as fine even when it isn't.

items.text: “My mother ran the house like a clock. She never sat down while the rest of us ate.”
items.why: Nobody tells Gran to do anything in this line. Her mother shows her how, by doing it in front of her. Showing a child how to follow a message is the program, and here it teaches the good one how to serve and never sit.

items.text: “I'll live properly once the children are settled.”
items.why: This one is the plan itself. It puts the living behind a condition, and that is the decision she made and has kept.

items.text: “I make his tea at four, sweet, the way he likes it.”
items.why: A present choice, kind and freely made. It doesn't come from a message she got as a girl, so it isn't part of the Plan.

items.cue: said at the lift, and she is pleased and also tired
items.why: The praise is for being strong, which is a Must. Being pleased is the reward, and being tired is the cost. The Must keeps earning the praise, so it keeps running.

traps.1: This would be hurry up if the praise were about speed, as in 'you get everything done so fast'. Nobody praises her for speed in the story, only for holding on.
traps.2: This would be try hard if the praise were about effort, as in 'you keep trying so hard'. The praise is about strength, and strength is what the Must is for.

items.example: A school prize day. The headmaster tells a boy who came first every year, “You're so strong, you never need help,” and the boy stops asking for help in class.

items.text: “I put it under the newspaper and said I'd look later.”
items.cue: read from her story, about the drawing with twelve wheels
items.why: The drawing is pushed out of sight and called later. The Don't that Gran passes on to Leo is don't be important: what a child makes doesn't count.

traps.1: This would be don't feel if Gran had cried over the drawing. There are no tears here. She puts the drawing away and moves on, and what that says is about worth.
traps.2: This would be don't be close if she had pushed him away from the table. Leo is still at her side, and what goes is the drawing.

items.example: A family group chat, Sunday. A father posts a photo of his son's model rocket, and the reply is “Nice. Now delete it, the group is full.”

items.text: “Mum, do the sewing class. I'll pay the fee, and you don't have to ask me first.”
items.cue: a Sunday call from Canada, Gran on speaker by the kettle
items.why: A permission. It says Gran may do the thing she keeps putting off, and the fee comes with the line. Nothing in it asks her to be good first.

traps.0: A Don't would shut a door, like “Stay home where I can see you.” This line opens one, and it pays for the way in.
traps.1: A Must would set a condition, like “Be the good one.” This line has no condition in it, and nobody is keeping score.

items.example:
A family WhatsApp group, Sunday.
Your brother: “Go on, book the trip. I'll cover the hotel.”
Nobody asks what you did to deserve it. He has said yes, and he has put money behind it.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: The boss runs harder. The lines have more beats, and some of the kindest-sounding options keep the trap running. Watch what each line does to Gran's chair.

items.title: Saturday, the pudding and the list
items.setting: Saturday, 4:05pm. Apartment 1A, Gran's kitchen. Leo is at the window. He is drawing a bus. The Heckler, in your head: 'Don't make a fuss. Let her finish the pudding.'

beats.text: “I'm sixty-four, my knees are bad, and the children are not settled. I'll live once they are, I suppose.”
beats.cue: stirring the pudding, not looking up

lines.text: “Gran, what's one thing you'd do this month if it needed nobody's permission but yours?”
lines.outcome: She stops stirring. 'Nothing. There's Leo, the building society, the knees.' But she has heard the question.
lines.why: A question that puts the choice in her hands. Her line is about waiting, and this question asks her to act on something this month.

lines.text: “That's sad, Gran. Still, the children will settle one day.”
lines.outcome: She nods and goes back to stirring. The wait is kept, and the afternoon goes on.
lines.why: It sounds kind, but it agrees the wait is fine. The Plan is safe when someone agrees with it.

lines.text: “Oh Gran, you've carried everyone. Sit down, I'll finish the pudding. You've done enough.”
lines.outcome: She sits, and the spoon is in your hand. 'Well, you've done enough,' she says, and the pudding goes cold.
lines.why: A trap move. It looks like help, but it takes her out of the chair she could stand up from. 'Sit down, you've done enough' also repeats her mother's Don't. It ends the scene early.

beats.text: “Nothing. I haven't got time for a list. There's Leo, the building society, my knees.”
beats.cue: pointing the spoon at the window

lines.text: “You're allowed to start the list now, Gran. Pick the smallest thing and put a day on it.”
lines.outcome: 'The smallest thing,' she says slowly. 'The class at the hall, on a Thursday, maybe.'
lines.why: A permission and a small, dated step. The list grew one 'later' at a time. A day on it makes it a plan she can act on.

lines.text: “Maybe next year, when things calm down.”
lines.outcome: 'Next year,' she says, and the list stays on the shelf.
lines.why: Next year is another condition. The Plan just moves the finish line again.

beats.text: “The class is at the community hall. My daughter says I should go, but she says it on the phone and then forgets.”
beats.cue: turning off the gas, one hand on her hip

lines.text: “Then ring her and say it plainly. Tell her Thursday at ten, and ask her to ring you on Friday to hear how it went.”
lines.outcome: 'She'll say I'm being silly,' Gran says. 'Still, she'll ring.'
lines.why: A clear plan with a net under it: a fixed day and time, plus someone to check in. The green light comes with the net, so the step is less likely to be dropped.

lines.outcome: The phone call stays in the future, along with the class.
lines.why: Agreeing with the daughter's vagueness keeps the plan vague, and a vague plan never gets a day.

beats.text: “Gran, can I come on Thursday? I'll draw in the hall.”
beats.cue: pencil in the air, looking at Gran, not at you

lines.text: “That's a good plan, Leo. Ask her yourself, and tell her what you'll draw.”
lines.outcome: Leo turns to her. 'I'll draw a bus. With twelve wheels.' Gran looks up for the first time since the pudding.
lines.why: You send the question back to the person who can answer it, and Leo gets to be important for a minute. The Don't loses some of its grip when a child asks for something and is heard.

lines.outcome: Leo shrugs and goes back to the window. Gran doesn't look up.
lines.why: It is correct in form and cold in tone. The one child in the room is sent off, and the Don't keeps working.

beats.text: “Thursday, the hall, at ten. I suppose the children can manage one hour without me.”
beats.cue: not looking at the pudding, looking at Leo

lines.text: “That's a new line, Gran. Say it once more, the one about the children managing.”
lines.outcome: 'The children can manage one hour without me,' she says, and she laughs at herself.
lines.why: Naming the new line out loud makes it hers. Repeating it helps her hear it as a plan she can keep.

lines.outcome: She eats one spoon and says the pudding has gone cold.
lines.why: Kind, but it lets the new line slide past. The plan needs to be heard once more.

items.payoff: Gran sits, and the pudding goes cold. The old line wins again: I'll live once the children are settled. You helped it win by doing the work for her.
items.example: A neighbour's mother who says “After the wedding” about the holiday she wants. The day after the wedding, it is “After the baby.”

items.text: “Gran needs a new line, one she can say today. Which one is a real rewrite of the line, and not the old Plan in a new coat?”
items.cue: turning the blank Plan Board round to face you
options: I'll live properly once the children are settled.
I'll start on Thursday at the hall, and the children can manage an hour without me.
I'll rest after Leo's exams are over, and then I'll decide.
items.why: A rewritten line is one she can say today and act on. The second option names a day and a place, and the line is hers. The first is the old line, and the third moves the condition again, which is the old Plan with a new date on it.

traps.0: This is the old line, word for word. Saying it again would keep the wait in place, and Gran would leave the board exactly as it was.
traps.2: This sounds like progress, but it moves the condition to Leo's exams. Gran would have a new finish line and the same wait, and the Thursday hall would still be empty.

items.example: A retired bank clerk who said “Once the grandchildren are older, I'll learn the violin.” She booked a Tuesday class instead and rang her sister to say so.

items.text: “Put Gran's Musts and Don'ts together. Which line is the decision underneath them?”
items.cue: running a finger down the board, then tapping the last box
options: My life starts once the others are taken care of.
I must always look strong in front of the neighbours.
I'll always be the one who makes the tea.
items.why: The books call this the script decision: the choice a child makes between her own needs and the pressure of the messages around her, which then steers the rest of the Plan. The Don'ts and Musts are the material. The decision itself is that her life starts once the others are looked after, and she has kept it since she was small.

traps.1: This reading would send the talk to looking strong and the neighbours, and it would stop at the family's pride. The decision under it, about her own life, would go unnoticed.
traps.2: This reading would send the talk to tea. It is a loving habit, but the decision costing her years is somewhere else.

items.example: A neighbour who ran the family accounts for thirty years and says he never had time for a hobby. The hobby kit is still in the box in the loft.

items.text: “Your new line is only a wish until something holds it up. What helps a person revoke an old decision and make a new one?”
items.cue: pushing the sheet back across the table to Gran's side
options: A promise to feel differently by next year.
A present choice she can act on this month, with permission and protection under it.
A clever argument that proves the old line was wrong.
items.why: The books call this revoking the old decision, or redecision. Permission lets a person go against the old message, and protection keeps her from sliding back when she feels alone and frightened. A promise to feel differently has no step in it, and an argument alone seldom moves a plan.

traps.0: This answer would have Gran wait for a feeling next year. The Until line would stay exactly where it is.
traps.2: This answer would give Gran a debate and nothing to do on Thursday. A clever argument can win the room and still leave her at home.

items.example: A football coach tells a boy who always apologises, “You may take the free kick. I'll stand by the goal if you miss.” The permission and the net are both in the sentence.

debrief.nadia: Gran made her decision as a girl, and she has kept it for more than fifty years. Her mother and father gave her the Don'ts and the Musts, her mother showed her how, and she did the rest herself, which was the waiting. Your own Plan Board is the same kind of drawing, and the line on it can be written again.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this the script matrix: a diagram of the messages each parent sends, the Musts from the parent's Parent, the Don'ts from the parent's Child and the how-to the same-sex parent shows, and the decision the child makes in answer.

reflection.prompt: Now build your own Plan Board from your choices so far. Which Don't sits under the Must you use most, and what did it cost you the last time it ran?
